Satisfied
SAT-is-fyde
v. (past part.)
From Latin satis, enough, and facere, to make — to make enough. Webster 1828: to gratify wants, wishes or desires to the full extent; to free from doubt; to pay to content. The theological weight of the word is in Isaiah 53:11, where it is the Servant who is satisfied, and in the Reformed doctrine of satisfaction that answers to it.

Biblical Definition

Satisfied in Scripture is almost always a verdict on where a soul has looked for its fill. The negative case is stated as a law of nature: Hell and destruction are never full; so the eyes of man are never satisfied (Proverbs 27:20). Ecclesiastes says the same of money, and the whole book is an experiment proving it. Against that stands the psalmist’s single answer, which is not a different quantity but a different object: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness (Psalm 17:15). Not with plenty, not with vindication, and not in this life — when I awake, with Thy likeness. The table of the covenant meets it in this world in part: My soul shall be satisfied as with marrow and fatness (Psalm 63:5), and the meek shall eat and be satisfied (Psalm 22:26), a verse from the psalm of the cross. And underneath all of it lies the sentence that governs the doctrine of the atonement: He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied: by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many; for he shall bear their iniquities (Isaiah 53:11). The satisfaction of the Servant is the ground of every other satisfaction Scripture offers a sinner.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SATISFY as to gratify wants or desires to the full; to supply fully; to free from doubt or suspense; and, in law and divinity, to pay or discharge a debt or penalty — the sense that gives the Reformed doctrine of satisfaction its name.

expand to see more

SATISFY, v.t. — To gratify wants, wishes or desires to the full extent; to supply fully what is desired.

To free from doubt, suspense or uncertainty; to convince, as by evidence.

To pay to content; to discharge, as a claim or a penalty; to make satisfaction for an offense.

SATISFACTION, n. — That which satisfies; amends; atonement for a crime; the payment of a penalty due.

Webster’s legal sense is the one Anselm and the Reformed divines use: Christ’s death is a satisfaction to divine justice, not merely an influence upon men.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 53:11 — "He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied: by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many; for he shall bear their iniquities."

Psalm 17:15 — "As for me, I will behold thy face in righteousness: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness."

Psalm 22:26 — "The meek shall eat and be satisfied: they shall praise the LORD that seek him: your heart shall live for ever."

Psalm 63:5 — "My soul shall be satisfied as with marrow and fatness; and my mouth shall praise thee with joyful lips:"

Proverbs 27:20 — "Hell and destruction are never full; so the eyes of man are never satisfied."

Modern Corruption

Satisfaction has been relocated from God to the self. The modern question is whether a man is satisfied with his life; Scripture’s question is whether God has been satisfied concerning his sin, and the answer at Calvary settles the other one.

expand to see more

Therapeutic religion treats satisfaction as an internal state to be cultivated: contentment practices, gratitude exercises, the management of expectation. Some of that is common-sense wisdom and Scripture has its own version of it, since Paul learned in whatsoever state he was therewith to be content. But Proverbs 27:20 says the eye cannot be trained to be full, because the appetite is not a habit but a hunger, and hell itself is the standard of comparison. No discipline satisfies an infinite capacity with finite objects. Psalm 17:15 answers with an object rather than a technique, and defers the fulness to the resurrection: when I awake, with thy likeness. Any spirituality that promises the fulness now, without the waking, is promising what the psalmist did not.

The graver corruption is the loss of the objective doctrine. Modern theories of the atonement — moral influence, Christus Victor made exclusive, governmental theories — all move the transaction away from God’s justice being satisfied and toward something happening in man or in the cosmos. Isaiah 53:11 has the Servant satisfied at the sight of the travail of His soul, and the reason given is that he shall bear their iniquities. Sin was borne, justice was answered, and the One who bore it is content with what He purchased. That is why the doctrine of definite atonement matters pastorally: a satisfaction actually rendered for actual persons is a finished thing, and the believer’s peace rests on a completed payment rather than on a possibility.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew saba (H7646), to be sated or filled; Greek chortazo (G5526), to feed to the full; the doctrinal noun is Latin satisfactio, a making-enough.

expand to see more

Hebrew saba (H7646) — to be satisfied, sated, filled; Psalm 17:15, 22:26, 63:5, Proverbs 27:20.

Hebrew sobah (H7648) — satiety, fulness; the noun of the same root.

Greek chortazo (G5526) — to feed, to fill; Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled (Matthew 5:6).

Latin satis facere — to make enough; whence satisfaction, the classical Reformed term for Christ’s work Godward.

Isaiah 53:11 reads literally that from the travail of His soul He shall see and be satisfied — the Servant’s own contentment with the result of His suffering.

Usage

"He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied (Isaiah 53:11) — the Servant content with what His death purchased."

"I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness (Psalm 17:15) — fulness deferred to the resurrection."

"The eyes of man are never satisfied (Proverbs 27:20) — the appetite measured against hell."
